intro.x: Brownian motion is the continuous-time, continuous-space limit of the simple random walk of Chapter 12, and the basic building block of continuous-time models. In this chapter we construct it as a scaling limit, derive its key properties, and build the It^o calculus needed to work with functions of it.

sections.title: From random walks to Brownian motion

blocks.x: Let $S_k=\xi_1+\dots+\xi_k$ be a simple symmetric random walk. Rescale time by $n$ and space by $\sqrt n$:
B^{(n)}_t=\frac{S_{\lfloor nt\rfloor}}{\sqrt n},\qquad t\ge0 .

For fixed $t$, the CLT (Chapter 11) gives $B^{(n)}_t\xrightarrow{d}N(0,t)$. For $s<t$, the increments $B^{(n)}_t-B^{(n)}_s$ and $B^{(n)}_s$ are independent (they use disjoint steps), and the increment is approximately $N(0,t-s)$. These observations motivate the definition.
A standard Brownian motion (Wiener process) is a process $(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ with
independent increments: for $0\le t_0
Gaussian stationary increments: $B_t-B_s\sim N(0,t-s)$ for $s
continuous paths: $t\mapsto B_t$ is continuous almost surely.

The existence of such a process (the hard part is (iv)) is established by the L'evy–Ciesielski construction or via Donsker’s theorem (both cited): the process $B^{(n)}$, with linear interpolation, converges in distribution on $C[0,\infty)$ to Brownian motion. This is the functional CLT: it says that any functional of the path that is continuous (maximum, hitting times, integrals) of a random walk is asymptotically the same functional of $B$.
$(B_t)$ is a Gaussian process with $\Exp[B_t]=0$ and $\Cov(B_s,B_t)=\min(s,t)$. Conversely a continuous centered Gaussian process with this covariance is a Brownian motion.

For $s\le t$, $B_t=B_s+(B_t-B_s)$ with independent summands, so $\Cov(B_s,B_t)=\Var(B_s)+0=s$. Any finite collection $(B_{t_1},\dots,B_{t_n})$ is a linear image of the independent Gaussian increments, hence jointly Gaussian (Chapter 8). For the converse, a Gaussian vector is determined by its mean and covariance; the increments of such a process have covariance $\Cov(B_{t_{i+1}}-B_{t_i},B_{t_{j+1}}-B_{t_j})= \min(\cdot)-\dots=0$ for disjoint intervals, hence are independent (uncorrelated jointly Gaussian), and have variance $t-s$.
If $B$ is a Brownian motion then so are: (a) $-B$; (b) $B_{t+h}-B_h$ (Markov / time-shift); (c) $c^{-1/2}B_{ct}$ for $c>0$ (scaling); (d) $tB_{1/t}$ with value $0$ at $t=0$ (time inversion).

In each case the process is Gaussian with continuous paths (continuity at $0$ for (d) follows from the strong law $B_s/s\to0$), mean zero, and covariance (a) $\min(s,t)$; (b) $\Cov(B_{s+h}-B_h,B_{t+h}-B_h)=\min(s+h,t+h)-h=\min(s,t)$; (c) $c^{-1}\min(cs,ct)=\min(s,t)$; (d) $st\min(1/s,1/t)=\min(s,t)$. Proposition 16.2 identifies each as a Brownian motion.
For $\Pi_n:0=t_0<\dots<t_n=T$ with mesh $\to0$ (take equal spacing $T/n$),
\sum_{i}(B_{t_{i+1}}-B_{t_i})^2\xrightarrow{L^2}T .

The terms $X_i=(B_{t_{i+1}}-B_{t_i})^2$ are independent with $\Exp X_i=\Delta_i:=t_{i+1}-t_i$ and $\Var X_i=2\Delta_i^2$ (fourth moment of a normal: $\Exp Z^4=3\sigma^4$, so $\Var=3\sigma^4-\sigma^4$). Therefore the sum has mean $T$ and variance $2\sum\Delta_i^2\le2T\max\Delta_i\to0$.

Almost surely, Brownian paths have infinite total variation on every interval; hence they cannot be differentiable on any interval of positive length (a differentiable path has finite total variation).

If $V$ is the total variation on $[0,T]$ (a.s. finite on an event of positive probability) then $\sum(\Delta B)^2\le\max_i\abs{\Delta B_i}\cdot V\to0$ along a sequence for which the sum converges a.s. (a subsequence from $L^2$ convergence), by uniform continuity of paths, contradicting the limit $T>0$.

Quadratic variation is the origin of the unusual rule of Brownian calculus: in a Taylor expansion, $(\Delta B)^2$ is not negligible—it is of order $\Delta t$, like the first-order term in time. Ordinary calculus discards second-order terms; It^o calculus cannot. This one fact is the source of the extra term in It^o’s lemma.

sections.title: The reflection principle and hitting times

blocks.x: Let $T_a=\inf\{t:B_t=a\}$ for $a>0$. We use the strong Markov property (cited, as the continuous analogue of Chapter 12): for any stopping time $\tau<\infty$, $(B_{\tau+t}-B_\tau)_{t\ge0}$ is a Brownian motion independent of the past up to $\tau$.
For $a>0$ and $t>0$,
\Prob(T_a\le t)=\Prob\Bigl(\max_{s\le t}B_s\ge a\Bigr)=2\Prob(B_t\ge a)=2\Bigl(1-\Phi(a/\sqrt t)\Bigr).

Condition on $T_a=s\le t$. After $T_a$, the process $B_{T_a+u}-a$ is a Brownian motion, symmetric about $0$, so $\Prob(B_t\ge a\given T_a=s)=\Prob(B_t\le a\given T_a=s)=\tfrac12$. Since $\{B_t\ge a\}\subseteq\{T_a\le t\}$ (continuity of paths), $\Prob(B_t\ge a)=\Prob(T_a\le t,B_t\ge a)=\tfrac12\Prob(T_a\le t)$.
$T_a$ has density $f_{T_a}(t)=\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2\pi t^3}}e^{-a^2/2t}$, $\Prob(T_a<\infty)=1$, and $\Exp[T_a]=\infty$. The maximum $M_t=\max_{s\le t}B_s$ has the same law as $\abs{B_t}$.

Differentiate $2(1-\Phi(a/\sqrt t))$ in $t$: with $\Phi'=\phi$, $\frac d{dt}=-2\phi(a/\sqrt t)\cdot\bigl(-\tfrac a2t^{-3/2}\bigr)=\frac{a}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,t^{3/2}}e^{-a^2/2t}$. Letting $t\to\infty$, $\Prob(T_a\le t)\to2\cdot\tfrac12=1$. Tail: $\Prob(T_a>t)=2\Phi(a/\sqrt t)-1\sim a\sqrt{2/(\pi t)}$, which is not integrable, hence $\Exp T_a=\int_0^\infty\Prob(T_a>t)dt=\infty$. Finally $\Prob(M_t\ge a)=2\Prob(B_t\ge a)=\Prob(\abs{B_t}\ge a)$.

blocks.name: Interview check
blocks.title: Brownian motion hits every level, but takes infinite expected time

blocks.x: Recurrence: $\Prob(T_a<\infty)=1$ for all $a$, yet $\Exp[T_a]=\infty$. This is the continuous analogue of the null recurrence of the symmetric random walk (Chapter 12). Via optional stopping one shows, for the two-sided exit time $\tau$ of $(-a,b)$: $\Prob(B_\tau=b)=a/(a+b)$ and $\Exp[\tau]=ab$ (the martingales $B_t$ and $B_t^2-t$).
Let $\tau=\inf\{t:B_t\in\{-a,b\}\}$ with $a,b>0$. Then $\Prob(B_\tau=b)=\dfrac a{a+b}$ and $\Exp[\tau]=ab$.

$B_{t\wedge\tau}$ is a bounded martingale, so optional stopping gives $0=\Exp B_\tau=b\,p-a(1-p)$, i.e. $p=a/(a+b)$. The process $B_t^2-t$ is a martingale (from $\Exp[B_t^2-B_s^2\given\F_s]=t-s$). Optional stopping at $t\wedge\tau$ gives $\Exp[B_{t\wedge\tau}^2]=\Exp[t\wedge\tau]$; let $t\to\infty$: the left side tends to $\Exp[B_\tau^2]=b^2p+a^2(1-p)=ab$ by bounded convergence, and the right side to $\Exp\tau$ by monotone convergence.

We want to define $\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ for a process $H$ adapted to the filtration $\F_t=\sigma(B_s:s\le t)$ (so $H_s$ depends only on the past). Since $B$ has infinite variation, Riemann–Stieltjes integration fails; we use $L^2$ limits.
Step 1: simple integrands

If $H_s=\sum_{i}h_i\indic_{(t_i,t_{i+1}]}(s)$ with $h_i$ $\F_{t_i}$-measurable and bounded, define $\int_0^tH\,dB=\sum_ih_i(B_{t_{i+1}\wedge t}-B_{t_i\wedge t})$—the left endpoint is used, the discrete martingale transform of Chapter 14.
For simple $H$, $I_t=\int_0^tH\,dB$ is a martingale and
\Exp\Bigl[\Bigl(\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s\Bigr)^2\Bigr]=\Exp\int_0^tH_s^2\,ds .

Write $\Delta_i=B_{t_{i+1}}-B_{t_i}$. For $i<j$, $h_ih_j\Delta_i$ is $\F_{t_j}$-measurable and $\Delta_j$ is independent of $\F_{t_j}$ with mean $0$, so $\Exp[h_ih_j\Delta_i\Delta_j]=0$. Hence $\Exp[I^2]=\sum_i\Exp[h_i^2\Delta_i^2]=\sum_i\Exp[h_i^2]\,(t_{i+1}-t_i)=\Exp\int H^2ds$. The martingale property: $\Exp[h_i\Delta_i\given\F_{t_i}]=h_i\Exp[\Delta_i]=0$.
Step 2: extension

The isometry says that $H\mapsto\int H\,dB$ is an isometry from simple processes in $L^2(\Omega\times[0,t])$ to $L^2(\Omega)$. Any adapted $H$ with $\Exp\int_0^tH^2ds<\infty$ is an $L^2$ limit of simple processes (cited density argument), so the integral extends uniquely to such $H$, continuing to be a martingale with the same isometry. For example, using left-endpoint sums one finds
\int_0^tB_s\,dB_s=\tfrac12B_t^2-\tfrac12t .

With equal partition, $\sum B_{t_i}(B_{t_{i+1}}-B_{t_i})=\tfrac12\sum\bigl(B_{t_{i+1}}^2-B_{t_i}^2\bigr)-\tfrac12\sum(B_{t_{i+1}}-B_{t_i})^2$, using $a(b-a)=\tfrac12(b^2-a^2)-\tfrac12(b-a)^2$. The first sum telescopes to $\tfrac12B_t^2$, the second converges in $L^2$ to $\tfrac12t$ (Theorem 16.4).

The ordinary calculus answer would be $\tfrac12B_t^2$. The extra $-\tfrac12t$ arises because the left-endpoint rule (It^o) differs from the midpoint rule (Stratonovich, which gives $\tfrac12B_t^2$) by exactly the quadratic variation. Using the left endpoint makes the integral a martingale and models “you choose the bet before seeing the increment”.
Let $f\in C^{1,2}$ (once differentiable in $t$, twice in $x$). Then
f(t,B_t)=f(0,0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(f_t+\tfrac12f_{xx}\Bigr)(s,B_s)\,ds+\int_0^tf_x(s,B_s)\,dB_s ,
or in differential form $df=(f_t+\tfrac12f_{xx})dt+f_x\,dB$.
For a partition, Taylor’s theorem gives
f(t_{i+1},B_{t_{i+1}})-f(t_i,B_{t_i})\approx f_t\Delta t+f_x\Delta B+\tfrac12f_{xx}(\Delta B)^2+\text{(smaller terms)} .

Sum over $i$. The $f_x\Delta B$ terms sum to the It^o integral. The terms $\tfrac12f_{xx}(\Delta B_i)^2$ behave, by the argument of Theorem 16.4 (their conditional mean given the past is $\tfrac12f_{xx}\Delta t_i$ and the fluctuation has variance of order $\sum\Delta t_i^2\to0$), like $\tfrac12f_{xx}\Delta t_i$, which sum to $\int\tfrac12f_{xx}ds$. The terms $\Delta t\,\Delta B$ and $(\Delta B)^3$ are of order $\Delta t^{3/2}$, summing to $O(\max\Delta t^{1/2})\to0$. Making the error control rigorous requires a localisation argument (cited).
Take $f(x)=x^2$: $d(B^2)=dt+2B\,dB$, i.e. $B_t^2=t+2\int_0^tB\,dB$, matching the direct computation above.
Let $S_t=S_0\exp\bigl((\mu-\tfrac12\sigma^2)t+\sigma B_t\bigr)$. Applying It^o to $f(t,x)=S_0e^{(\mu-\sigma^2/2)t+\sigma x}$: $f_t=(\mu-\tfrac12\sigma^2)f$, $f_x=\sigma f$, $f_{xx}=\sigma^2f$, so
dS_t=\bigl(\mu-\tfrac12\sigma^2+\tfrac12\sigma^2\bigr)S_t\,dt+\sigma S_t\,dB_t=\mu S_t\,dt+\sigma S_t\,dB_t .

Hence $S_t$ solves the stochastic differential equation $dS=\mu S\,dt+\sigma S\,dB$, the standard model of a stock price with drift $\mu$ and volatility $\sigma$. Its mean is $\Exp S_t=S_0e^{\mu t}$ (the lognormal MGF: $\Exp e^{\sigma B_t}=e^{\sigma^2t/2}$), although the typical (median) path grows at the lower rate $\mu-\tfrac12\sigma^2$.

For $\mu<\tfrac12\sigma^2$, $S_t\to0$ almost surely (since $B_t/t\to0$ and the exponent $\to-\infty$) while $\Exp S_t=S_0e^{\mu t}$ may still grow. The mean is carried by rare, enormous paths. This is the same phenomenon as the betting paradoxes of Chapter 14: for repeated multiplicative bets the long-run growth rate is the expectation of the log, not the log of the expectation.

sections.title: Black–Scholes: pricing by a no-arbitrage argument

blocks.x: Consider a market with a riskless asset growing at rate $r$ and a stock $S$ following GBM. A derivative paying $g(S_T)$ at time $T$ has price $V(t,S_t)$ for a function $V$. By It^o,
dV=\bigl(V_t+\mu SV_S+\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS}\bigr)dt+\sigma SV_S\,dB .
Form the portfolio that is short one derivative and long $V_S$ shares ($\Delta$-hedge). Its value changes by
d\Pi=-dV+V_S\,dS=-\bigl(V_t+\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS}\bigr)dt ,
because the $dB$ terms and the $\mu$ terms cancel: the portfolio is riskless. To avoid arbitrage it must earn the riskless rate: $d\Pi=r\Pi\,dt=r(-V+SV_S)\,dt$. Equating,
V_t+\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS}+rSV_S-rV=0,\qquad V(T,S)=g(S) ,
the Black–Scholes PDE, in which the drift $\mu$ has disappeared. By the Feynman–Kac formula (cited) its solution is
V(t,S)=e^{-r(T-t)}\,\Exp^{\mathbb Q}[g(S_T)\given S_t=S],
where under the risk-neutral measure $\mathbb Q$ the stock has drift $r$ instead of $\mu$. For a call $g(S)=(S-K)^+$ this evaluates to
C=S\,\Phi(d_1)-Ke^{-r\tau}\Phi(d_2),\quad d_{1,2}=\frac{\ln(S/K)+(r\pm\tfrac12\sigma^2)\tau}{\sigma\sqrt\tau},\ \tau=T-t .

Under $\mathbb Q$, $S_T=Se^{(r-\sigma^2/2)\tau+\sigma\sqrt\tau Z}$, $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Then $\Exp[(S_T-K)^+]=\Exp[S_T\indic_{S_T>K}]-K\Prob(S_T>K)$. The event $S_T>K$ is $Z>-d_2$, so $\Prob(S_T>K)=\Phi(d_2)$. For the first term, completing the square, $\Exp[e^{\sigma\sqrt\tau Z}\indic_{Z>-d_2}]=e^{\sigma^2\tau/2}\Prob(Z+\sigma\sqrt\tau>-d_2)=e^{\sigma^2\tau/2}\Phi(d_2+\sigma\sqrt\tau)=e^{\sigma^2\tau/2}\Phi(d_1)$, so that term equals $Se^{r\tau}\Phi(d_1)$. Discount by $e^{-r\tau}$.

The price depends on $\sigma$ but not on the investors’ belief $\mu$. The reason is replication: the hedge removes all risk, so no expectation under the real-world measure is needed. Risk-neutral probabilities are a pricing device (a change of measure, via Girsanov’s theorem, cited), not forecasts.
Show that $B_t^3-3tB_t$ is a martingale. Hint: use It^o’s lemma, or direct computation of $\Exp[B_t^3-3tB_t\given\F_s]$.
Find $\Exp[\tau^2]$-type information: show that $\Var(\tau)$ for the exit time of $(-a,a)$ is $\tfrac23a^4$, using the martingale $B_t^4-6tB_t^2+3t^2$.
Show $\Exp\bigl[B_t^4\bigr]=3t^2$ using It^o’s lemma.
Compute $\Cov(B_s,\int_0^tB_u\,du)$.
Using the reflection principle, find the density of the last zero before time $1$ (arcsine law): $\Prob(\text{no zero in }(s,1))$ and deduce $\frac2\pi\arcsin\sqrt s$.
Prove that $e^{\theta B_t-\theta^2t/2}$ is a martingale for every $\theta$, and use it to re-derive $\Exp[e^{-\lambda T_a}]=e^{-a\sqrt{2\lambda}}$.
Show that $\Prob(T_a<T_{-b})=b/(a+b)$ and compare with gambler’s ruin (Chapter 12).
For the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck equation $dX=-\theta X\,dt+\sigma\,dB$, apply It^o to $e^{\theta t}X_t$ and solve for $X_t$; find the stationary distribution.
